section.title: Our Great High Priest
section.sectionRationale: These three verses are the hinge of the letter, gathering the high priest theme introduced in chapter 2 and launching the sustained argument of chapters 5 to 10. Because Jesus is both exalted through the heavens and able to sympathize with our weakness, believers are called to hold fast and to draw near boldly to the throne of grace.
section.thesis: Jesus, the Son of God, is our great high priest who has passed through the heavens and yet was tempted in every way as we are, without sin; therefore we should hold firmly to our confession and approach the throne of grace with confidence, to receive mercy and timely grace.
section.frameNote: Two calls flowing from one great fact: because our high priest is both exalted and sympathetic, first hold firmly to what we profess, and then draw near with confidence to the throne of grace.

units.label: Hold fast: our exalted, sympathetic priest
units.note: tempted as we are, yet without sin

verses.text: Therefore, since we have a great {{archiereus|high priest}} who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold firmly to what we profess.
For we do not have a high priest who is unable to {{sympatheo|sympathize}} with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.

units.label: Draw near to the throne of grace

verses.text: Let us then approach the throne of grace with {{parresia|confidence}}, so that we may receive mercy and find {{charis|grace}} to help us in our time of need.

archiereus.gloss: High priest, the supreme mediator between God and the people. Jesus is the great high priest who has passed through the heavens into God's presence, uniting exaltation and nearness in a way no earthly priest ever could.

sympatheo.gloss: To suffer with, to feel alongside, to sympathize. Jesus is not a remote priest; having been tempted in every way, He feels with our weaknesses from the inside, so His help is that of one who truly understands.

parresia.gloss: Boldness, confidence, freedom of speech. Because of our high priest, we may come to God's throne not cowering but with confident freedom, speaking plainly as welcomed children rather than fearful strangers.

charis.gloss: Grace, undeserved favour and help. The throne we approach is a throne of grace, from which we receive mercy for our failures and grace precisely timed to help us in our moment of need.

basic.context: The writer has just described the word of God that exposes every heart. That could leave us afraid to come near God. But now comes the answer: we have a great high priest, Jesus, who has passed into heaven itself and yet knows our weakness from the inside, having been tempted as we are, without ever sinning. So we can come boldly to God's throne, which is a throne of grace, and find mercy and help.
basic.hermeneutics: These verses function as a pivot: 'therefore' looks back to the priest theme, and 'let us' twice looks forward to the exhortations that follow. Read them together: the exalted and sympathetic priest grounds both holding fast and drawing near.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus is our archiereus, high priest, who can sympatheō, sympathize, with our weakness. So we approach the throne with parrēsia, bold confidence, to receive charis, grace, that helps in time of need.
basic.typology: The high priest who once a year passed through the veil into the Most Holy Place foreshadows Jesus, who has passed through the heavens into God's presence. The mercy seat above the ark foreshadows the throne of grace we now approach.
basic.christ: Christ is the great high priest, fully God as the Son who has passed through the heavens, and fully able to sympathize as the man who was tempted in every way yet without sin. He is both exalted and near, and He opens the way to God's throne.
basic.god: God's throne, which might terrify us, is here called a throne of grace. God welcomes His people to come with confidence and dispenses mercy and well-timed grace to those in need.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 2 introduced the merciful high priest. Hebrews 10 urges us again to draw near with confidence. Romans 5 speaks of access into grace through Christ.
basic.oneStory: The whole priestly system pointed to a mediator who could bring people to God. In Christ that mediator has come, and the way to God's throne stands open.

context.literary:
These three verses are the hinge of the whole letter. Hebrews 4:14 and 10:23 form an inclusio around the central exposition: both open with the same summons to hold fast what we profess, and 4:16 is answered by 10:22, 'let us draw near.' Everything between, from 5:1 to 10:18, is the argument that makes those two calls reasonable. The writer announced the theme in 2:17 and 3:1, where Jesus is already 'merciful and faithful high priest' and 'high priest whom we confess,' and he now returns to it after the long exposition of rest and the word of God in 3:7 to 4:13.

The 'therefore' of verse 14 hooks backward, but the grammar of the two verses is balanced with care. Verse 14 states what we have, a great high priest who has passed through the heavens. Verse 15 states it again in the negative, 'we do not have a high priest who is unable,' a figure of speech that makes the positive claim land harder. Verse 16 then draws the result in a second 'let us.' The order is exaltation first, then nearness, then the invitation, so that the greatness of the priest is the very reason for the boldness of the approach.

The sentence also carries a quiet contrast with the passage just before it. Verses 12 and 13 describe a word that lays everything bare, and everything is 'uncovered and exposed' before God. The writer does not leave the reader exposed and trembling. He moves at once to a priest and a throne, so that the exposure of 4:13 is met by the mercy of 4:16.
context.historical:
The first readers knew the Day of Atonement. Once a year the high priest passed behind the veil with blood, and Leviticus 16:2 warned that he must not come in freely or he would die. Between the people and that presence stood the court, the altar, the Holy Place and a thick curtain. To hear that ordinary believers could approach the 'throne' with confidence would have sounded almost shocking.

The high priesthood in the first century also gave the claim a sharp edge. Under Roman rule the office was in the gift of political authority; high priests such as Annas and Caiaphas, named in Luke 3:2 and John 18:13, held it by appointment and could be removed. A letter that points to a priest whom God Himself has appointed, and who has gone through the heavens rather than a veil of cloth, speaks to people who may have felt the old system's glory fading or its leaders compromised.

The readers' circumstances matter too. Hebrews 10:32 to 34 recalls insults, imprisonment and the loss of property, and 12:4 says they had not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood. Pressed Jewish Christians could be tempted to retreat to a legally recognised synagogue life. The letter answers by saying they have something better than the temple: a priest who has already entered the real sanctuary and who knows pressure from the inside.

The authorship and exact date are unknown. The present tense used of the sacrifices in places such as 10:1 and 10:11 does not settle whether the temple still stood, and the argument does not depend on it.
context.canonical:
The idea of a priest who stands between God and people begins in Exodus 28 and 29 and is mapped out in Leviticus 16. The prophets also kept the hope alive that God would one day give a priest greater than Aaron. Psalm 110:4 swears one into being, and Zechariah 6:12 and 13 speaks of a Branch who will sit on His throne and be a priest on it. Hebrews reads these threads together.

The language of approach runs through the rest of the letter. The verb for drawing near appears of the law's inability to make worshippers perfect, 10:1, of the sincere heart in 10:22, and of the basic requirement of faith, 'anyone who comes to God must believe that He exists,' 11:6. It reaches its climax in 12:22, where believers 'have come to Mount Zion,' and in 12:28, which links the unshakable kingdom to grateful worship.

Elsewhere in the New Testament, Paul says we have access by faith into the grace in which we stand, Romans 5:2, and that through Christ both Jew and Gentile have access to the Father by one Spirit, Ephesians 2:18; Ephesians 3:12 speaks of boldness and confident access. Hebrews adds the picture of the throne and the priest. First John 2:1 gives a companion image, an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous One, and Romans 8:34 says that Christ is at God's right hand interceding for us.

Hebrews 4:15 also gathers up what the Gospels narrate: the wilderness testing of Matthew 4, and the anguish of Gethsemane, which Hebrews 5:7 will describe.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer is a pastor reaching for people who are wavering. He does not simply tell them to try harder. He gives them two reasons, and he places them in order. First, they have a priest who is beyond all rivals: He has already gone through the heavens, and He is Son of God. Second, that same priest is no distant official, for He has stood where they stand.

The point of verse 15 is not to define the exact mechanics of Jesus' inner life, but to remove a particular fear. The readers might think that a being so exalted could not understand how heavy their trial is. The writer says the opposite is true: the heavier the pressure, the more the sinless one has felt it, since only one who never gave in knows the full force of a temptation.

The response he wants is double. He wants them to hold on to their confession, which means to stay publicly with Christ when it costs them, and he wants them to come to God in prayer with an open, unembarrassed boldness. The two belong together. Those who do not draw near will not hold on, and those who truly draw near will find that they are held.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Verses 14 and 15 describe who Jesus is and what He has done; verse 16 and the opening of verse 14 prescribe what to do. The commands are in the first person plural, 'let us,' so the writer places himself under them too. They are an invitation to a shared practice of the church, not an order shouted from outside.

Two cautions help in application. First, the passage does not say that Jesus shared every sort of temptation in every detail, as though He must have faced each particular sin that a person today faces. It says He was tempted 'in every way' and 'without sin,' and the stress is on the reality and the pressure of the testing. Second, the throne of grace is not a licence. The aim is 'mercy' and 'grace to help' in a time of need, not permission to presume. Confidence here is not casual familiarity but trust that rests on a priest's work, which is why the same letter can say in 12:28 that worship should be offered with reverence and awe.

debates.question: How could Jesus be 'tempted in every way that we are' and yet be without sin?

views.label: Real temptation fully resisted
views.case: Jesus faced genuine temptation across the range of human experience and never yielded. Because He never gave way, He met its full force, in a way that one who yields early never does. Hebrews 2:18 says He 'suffered when He was tempted,' so the testing was costly, and the wilderness scenes of Matthew 4 and the garden of Luke 22:44 are the pictures the church has pointed to.

views.label: Sympathy grounded in shared human experience
views.case: The emphasis falls on His true humanity and solidarity with us. Whatever the mode of His temptation, He truly knew weakness and pressure, hunger, grief, rejection and fear, and so can feel with us. On this reading the phrase 'in every way' means in every kind of area, and need not claim that He met every possible instance.

debates.bearing: Either way His sinlessness qualifies rather than distances Him. He is a sympathetic helper precisely because He met temptation and did not fall.

debates.question: Could Jesus have sinned?

views.label: He was able not to sin, and was also able to sin
views.case: Some argue that if His temptations were to be real, sin must have been a genuine possibility, and His victory was a real victory of a human will upheld by the Spirit. They point to the language of testing and to Hebrews 5:8, where He 'learned' obedience through what He suffered.

views.label: He was unable to sin, though truly tempted
views.case: Others argue that because the person who was tempted is the eternal Son, sin was not possible for Him, and yet the temptation was still real, since an army can be attacked by a force it will never lose to. They stress His holiness in Hebrews 7:26, 'holy, innocent, undefiled,' and note that the weight of temptation is felt by the one who does not yield.

debates.bearing: The text asserts both facts, that He was truly tempted and that He was without sin, and it does not settle the metaphysics. What it does ask of the reader is to draw near to Him, not to explain Him away.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb of verse 14, 'hold firmly.' It is a verb of gripping, and the writer uses it again of laying hold of hope in 6:18 and of Christ as the head in Colossians 2:19. In both places it is present tense, which suggests a grip that is kept up, not a single act. What is gripped is the 'confession,' the public statement of faith, the word that appears in 3:1 and 10:23. To hold fast the confession is to refuse to take it back under pressure.

The verb 'passed through' is a perfect participle, dielelythota. It points to a completed journey whose result remains. Jesus has gone through the heavens, plural, and the same idea returns in 7:26, 'exalted above the heavens,' and 9:24, where He has entered 'heaven itself.' The Day of Atonement priest passed through a curtain; this priest has passed through the whole created order to the place where God dwells.

In verse 15 the phrase 'tempted in every way' joins a word for testing, which can mean either trial or temptation, with a phrase that is literally 'according to likeness.' The writer is not saying 'tempted by every single thing' but 'tempted in a way that matches ours.' The clause 'without sin' is short and flat; it does not excuse or explain. The word for sympathy, a verb that means to suffer with, returns in 10:34, where the readers themselves 'sympathized with those in prison.' The writer asks nothing of Christ that he has not already seen in them.

Verse 16 begins with a present-tense verb, 'let us approach,' that speaks of an ongoing coming near, not a single arrival. The verb is the standard one for approaching God, and it fills the letter: 7:25, 10:1, 10:22, 11:6 and 12:22. Alongside it stands the word translated 'confidence,' parrēsia, which in Hebrews is a possession we can keep or throw away: 3:6 says we are God's house if we hold firm our confidence, and 10:35 says 'do not throw away your confidence.' So the boldness of 4:16 is both a gift and a trust to be guarded.

The final clause says 'grace to help in our time of need.' 'Help' translates a word for coming to the aid of someone who cries out, and 'time of need' is literally a timely, well-timed help. The help arrives at the right moment, neither too early nor too late. Elsewhere Hebrews uses the related verb in 2:18, where Christ 'is able to help those who are being tempted.' The throne of verse 16 and the helper of 2:18 are the same Jesus.

typology.type: The high priest passing behind the veil, Leviticus 16:2
typology.fulfillment: On the Day of Atonement Aaron entered the Most Holy Place once a year, in a cloud of incense and with blood, and was warned that he must not come in freely or he would die. Hebrews 9:7 stresses that it was 'once a year,' and 9:24 says Christ entered 'heaven itself.' The escalation is that Jesus does not pass through a cloth veil but the heavens, 4:14, and does not leave again each year, since He sat down, 10:12. The type falls short because Aaron was a sinner who first offered for himself, Leviticus 16:6, while Jesus is without sin.

typology.type: The mercy seat above the ark, Exodus 25:17-22
typology.fulfillment: The golden cover of the ark was the place where God said, 'I will meet with you there,' Exodus 25:22, and where blood was sprinkled once a year. The throne of grace in Hebrews 4:16 is the same meeting place seen in its fulfilment. Hebrews 9:5 names the mercy seat and then says it cannot be discussed in detail, and Romans 3:25 speaks of Christ as the one God put forward as a propitiation, the same word family. The type falls short because the mercy seat was hidden from the people; the throne of grace is open to all who draw near.

typology.type: The priests who drew near to serve, Exodus 28:41
typology.fulfillment: Aaron and his sons were consecrated so they could serve God, and everyone else had to keep away. Numbers 18:22 warns that the people must not come near the tent. In Christ the privilege widens: believers are called 'a royal priesthood' in 1 Peter 2:9, and Hebrews 10:19 to 22 invites all of us to enter the sanctuary. The correspondence is that God's people still approach a holy presence through a priest. The escalation is that the priest has gone before us and carries us in, so that approach is no longer limited to one family or one day.

typology.type: The testing in the wilderness, Deuteronomy 8:2
typology.fulfillment: Israel was led through the wilderness forty years to be humbled and tested, to learn what was in her heart, and she failed more than once. Jesus, the true Son, was led into the wilderness for forty days and tested, and answered each time from Deuteronomy, Matthew 4:1 to 11. Hebrews has already linked His testing to Israel's in 3:7 to 4:13. The correspondence is that a Son is tested in the place where Israel fell. The escalation is that He holds firm. The type falls short because Israel needed her testing to expose sin, but His testing proved there was none.

study.christ:
This short passage does something no other part of the Bible does so plainly: it holds together the height and the nearness of Christ in a single sentence. He is 'great,' He has 'passed through the heavens,' and He is 'the Son of God,' and yet He is the one who has felt our weakness. Hebrews 1 has already shown the Son as radiance of God's glory and exact representation of His being, 1:3, and Hebrews 2:14 to 18 has shown that He shared our flesh and blood. Chapter 4 gathers those two lines and ties them to an office.

The title 'great high priest' needs to be read against the Old Testament. Aaron and his successors were 'high priests' of a human sort, who died and were replaced, Hebrews 7:23. This priest does not die, 7:24, and He does not need to offer for Himself first, 7:27. Hebrews therefore lets us feel the climb, from ordinary priests to a 'great' one, and then to one who is exalted above the heavens, 7:26.

The 'without sin' of 4:15 is not a footnote but the secret of His help. A priest who had sin of His own would need to deal with it before He could help anyone else, and Hebrews says this of Aaron in 5:3. Because Jesus has no such need, His full attention and power are turned to us. The same truth shows why He can 'save completely,' 7:25, and why He is able to keep on interceding.

The passage should also be read alongside Gethsemane and the cross. Hebrews 5:7 will remind us of the loud cries and tears, and 12:2 says He endured the cross, scorning its shame. The 'throne of grace' is where the crucified one now sits, and so grace is not an abstract favour but the fruit of a death. His sympathy is not an emotion kept in heaven; it was learned on earth.

Care is needed so that the text is not stretched. The passage does not say Jesus knew by experience the guilt of sin, only its pressure. It does not say He took the experience of every person. It says He is able to sympathize, and it says what follows from that: that we should come, hold on and receive. The links to the temple furniture and the Day of Atonement are Hebrews' own and are not our inventions.

What the passage gives, finally, is a Christ we can pray to. The invitation to approach is an invitation to speak to Him and, through Him, to the Father. When a believer comes in weakness, the one who answers is the one who has already endured it, and who will give mercy and timely help without reproach.
study.god:
The most striking thing this passage says about God is that His throne is described as a throne of grace. A throne is where a king judges and commands, and in the ancient world people approached one with fear. The Old Testament knew that God was holy and that His presence could be dangerous; Leviticus 16:2 is a warning of that. The writer does not deny that holiness. He says that, in Christ, the seat of God's rule is also the seat of His favour. The holy God and the gracious God are one God.

His grace is not given grudgingly. It is for 'mercy' and 'grace to help.' Mercy deals with what we have done, and help answers what we cannot do. Together they cover both our guilt and our weakness. That reflects what the Bible says of God elsewhere, that He is a God compassionate and gracious, as the LORD proclaimed His own name to Moses in Exodus 34:6.

God appears here as the one who designs access. He is not passive while we find our way. He appointed the priest, Hebrews 5:4 to 5, raised Him, and seated Him. The structure of verses 14 to 16 shows God providing both the way and the welcome. That is why the invitation can be a confident one: it rests on what He has done, not on how well we pray.

The passage also shows the Father's willingness to share His throne's access with ordinary people in 'time of need.' The phrase implies that He is attentive to particular moments, and that the help He gives is fitted to them. Passages such as Psalm 34:15 and Isaiah 65:24, in which God hears before the cry is finished, are in the background.

A tension is held without being resolved. God is exalted, 'passed through the heavens,' and God is near. He is holy and He welcomes sinners. He demands that we hold fast and He provides what lets us do it. The Bible does not weaken either side.

For worship, this means that prayer is not a last resort but a regular privilege. We come, as Hebrews 12:28 says, with reverence and awe, and also with confidence. The posture of a believer at the throne is neither a cringing nor a swagger: it is the bold, humble trust of one who knows that a priest has gone ahead and that the one on the throne is kind.

crossReferences.note: The first statement of the theme. Christ had to be made like His brothers in every way so that He might be a merciful and faithful high priest, and because He suffered when tempted, He is able to help the tempted. Hebrews 4:15 picks this up and sets it beside His exaltation.

The second half of the bracket. The same call to hold unswervingly to the hope we profess appears together with the call to draw near, here with the explicit ground of the blood of Jesus and the curtain of His body. What 4:16 invites, 10:19 explains.

God warns Aaron not to enter freely behind the veil, or he will die. The contrast makes the boldness of Hebrews 4:16 plain: what was forbidden at any time to every Israelite is now offered to all who come through Jesus.

At the mercy seat God promised to meet with Moses and speak with him above the cherubim. The throne of grace in Hebrews is the final form of that meeting place, no longer hidden in a tent but open to all who come.

Paul says we have been justified by faith, have peace with God, and have gained access into the grace in which we stand. It is the same idea as Hebrews 4:16, that access to grace is won by Christ and not earned by us.

In Christ and through faith in Him we may approach God with freedom and confidence. The two words of Hebrews 4:16, approach and confidence, appear together, showing that this was a shared apostolic teaching and not the writer's private idea.

The wilderness narrative is the clearest picture of the temptation Hebrews 4:15 has in mind. Jesus faces hunger, a demand for proof, and an offer of power, and each time He holds to the word of God. He is the one who knows by experience.

In Gethsemane Jesus prays in anguish, and an angel strengthens Him. The scene shows that His sympathy is not theoretical, and it prepares the loud cries and tears of Hebrews 5:7. Here the throne of grace is visited by the one who will sit on it.

John writes so that his readers will not sin, but adds that if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the Righteous One. It states in plain terms the pastoral comfort that Hebrews 4:15 and 16 give, that failure is met by a priest and not by a closed door.

Christ Jesus, who died and was raised, is at the right hand of God and is interceding for us. This is the work of the great high priest in action, and it is the reason a believer's approach does not depend on feeling confident.

Because He lives always to intercede, He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him. Verse 26 repeats the exalted and sinless character of 4:14 and 15, holy, innocent, undefiled and above the heavens.

The destination of the approach. Believers have come to Mount Zion, to the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant. Chapter 4's invitation to draw near is shown here as already true of the church.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who walks in a garden with the people He made, and the loss of that nearness is the central tragedy of Genesis 3. Cherubim and a flaming sword guard the way, Genesis 3:24. Every later priest, altar and veil is a way of living with that barrier: a means of approach that is real but limited. Hebrews 4:14 to 16 is the answer to that long loss.

The story's early priests were fathers and patriarchs offering sacrifices, and then at Sinai the work was given to Aaron's family, with a tent, a veil and a rule that only one man could go in, only one day a year. Under that arrangement Israel could never forget two things at once: God had drawn near to dwell among them, and sin kept them at a distance. The tabernacle was both promise and warning. The prophets then spoke of a day when God's presence would be known by all, Jeremiah 31:34, and when a priest would rise who was also a king, Psalm 110:4 and Zechariah 6:13.

In Jesus those lines meet. He is the priest who has gone through the heavens, who sits with the Father and who has felt our weakness. The exile east of Eden begins to be undone not by a return to a garden but by a new way into the presence of God. Through Him believers come to a throne and are not struck down.

The story is not yet finished. Believers still live in a world where they are tempted, weak and in need. That is why the passage speaks of holding fast and of a 'time of need.' The church lives between the entering of the priest and the appearing of the kingdom, 9:28, and during that time it prays at the throne of grace.

The ending in Revelation shows what is coming. The throne of God and of the Lamb stands in the city, and His servants will serve Him and see His face, Revelation 22:3 to 4. The barrier that began at Genesis 3 is gone. What the believer now does by faith, coming boldly to the throne, becomes sight, and the nearness that was lost in Eden is restored in full.

quiz.q: What two truths about Jesus ground the call to draw near?

options.text: He is exalted through the heavens and yet sympathizes with our weakness.
options.note: Verses 14 to 15 hold together His exaltation and His sympathy.

options.text: He is distant and unfamiliar with human life.
options.note: The opposite: He was tempted as we are and feels with us.

options.text: He is sympathetic but not truly exalted.
options.note: He is both; He has passed through the heavens as the Son of God.

options.text: He is exalted but unable to understand us.
options.note: He is exalted and also fully able to sympathize.

quiz.q: What does it mean that Jesus was tempted 'yet without sin'?

options.text: He faced real temptation at full strength and never yielded.
options.note: His sinlessness means He endured temptation fully, qualifying Him to help.

options.text: He was tempted yet, as the sinless Son, could not finally fail.
options.note: There is truth that He could not ultimately fail, yet the emphasis is that He met real temptation at full strength and truly sympathizes.

options.text: He sinned only in small, forgivable ways.
He was tempted but it did not really affect Him.
options.note: The temptation was genuine; He truly sympathizes with our weakness.

quiz.q: How are we to approach God's throne?

options.text: With confidence, to receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.
options.note: Verse 16 calls for bold, confident approach.
The throne is a throne of grace; we come with confidence.

options.text: Only through an earthly priest once a year.
options.note: Through Christ all believers may draw near freely.

options.text: Only after we have made ourselves worthy.
options.note: We come for mercy and help, not because we have made ourselves worthy.

quiz.q: What is the throne we approach called, and why does it matter?

options.text: A throne of grace, so we find mercy and help rather than condemnation.
options.note: God's throne is grace toward those who come through Christ.

options.text: A throne of terror to keep us away.
options.note: It might have terrified us, but through Christ it is a throne of grace.

options.text: A throne of pure law with no mercy.
options.note: It is explicitly a throne of grace giving mercy.

options.text: A throne reserved only for angels.
options.note: It is open to believers who draw near through their high priest.

questions: Jesus sympathizes with your weakness from the inside. How does that change what you feel able to bring to Him?
The throne of God is a throne of grace. Do you approach God more as a throne of grace or a throne of fear, and why?
We are invited to come with confidence. What holds you back from praying boldly and honestly?
Grace is promised to help 'in time of need'. Where do you need God's timely help right now, and will you ask?
Because our priest is both exalted and near, we are told to hold firmly to what we profess. What strengthens your grip on your confession when it is tested?

translationNotes.note: 'Passed through the heavens' pictures Jesus entering the very presence of God, surpassing the high priest who merely passed through the veil into the earthly Most Holy Place.
'Sympathize' translates a verb meaning to suffer or feel with another; it denotes fellow feeling grounded in shared experience, not mere pity from a distance.
'With confidence' renders parrēsia, boldness or freedom of speech; the same freedom of access is repeated in 10:19, framing the priestly section.
